cover.artAlt: A grand stone castle with tall towers glowing warm gold at sunset, framed by a moat and green hills
cover.blurb: As the sun sets gold over the moat, this castle is full of stories waiting for you. Turn the page to cross the drawbridge and step inside.

pages.title: A Suit Made of Steel
pages.artAlt: A shining suit of knight's armor stands on display in a museum

facts.text: A full suit of battle armor usually weighed about 45 to 55 pounds, about as heavy as a big packed suitcase. Because the weight was spread out over the knight's whole body, it felt much lighter than it sounds.

Museum tests with real armor show that a person in a well-fitted suit could run, lie down, get up again and even climb onto a horse without any help. One famous French knight could climb the underside of a ladder using only his hands while wearing full armor.
facts.artAlt: A person in a full polished steel suit of armor sitting on horseback at a tournament ground
facts.caption: A knight in full armor, up on his horse.

facts.text: Future knights started practicing young, and boys wore armor during training so they could get used to it. The Royal Armouries museum even looks after a suit of armor made for a six-year-old boy, and two more made for brothers aged eight and ten.
facts.artAlt: A very small child-sized suit of steel armor on a stand in a museum gallery
facts.caption: A suit of armor built for a boy.

infographic.title: How heavy is a suit of armor?

rows.label: A school backpack full of books
A full suit of battle armor

infographic.caption: The armor's weight comes from The Metropolitan Museum of Art. The everyday sizes are here only so you have something to measure against. Spread over a knight's whole body, it felt much lighter than it sounds.

pages.title: The Busiest Room in the Castle
pages.artAlt: Inside a castle's great hall, colorful banners hang above a long wooden table

facts.text: The great hall was the heart of the whole castle. The household gathered here to eat together at long tables with benches, because in a castle, mealtimes were something you shared with everyone.

Where you sat in the hall showed how important you were. The lord and the most special guests sat at the high table, placed at the end of the hall farthest from the kitchen, while everyone else sat in order down the long tables.
facts.artAlt: The inside of a castle great hall with a raised high table at the far end under a tall window
facts.caption: The high table sits at the far end of the hall, away from the kitchen.

facts.text: Castle meals were wonderfully slow. Lunch began at about 10 or 11 in the morning and could last two to three hours, with plenty of time for talking, music and second helpings.
facts.artAlt: A long medieval banquet table laid with wooden bowls, bread, roast food and cups
facts.caption: A castle lunch, laid out and ready.

infographic.title: Lunch in a great hall

pages.title: The Cleverest Front Door
pages.artAlt: A stone castle's drawbridge is lowered over a calm moat

facts.text: A castle entrance was a front door with moving parts. The castle's gatekeepers looked after the gate, a heavy sliding grille called a portcullis, and the drawbridge itself. With the bridge pulled up, the moat became a ring of water with no way across.

Some moats were truly enormous. At the Tower of London, King Edward I had a wide new moat dug right around the castle in the 1270s, and it was about 165 feet wide, which is about as wide as a football field.
facts.artAlt: A broad still moat running around the foot of a great stone castle wall, the towers reflected in the water
facts.caption: A wide moat wrapped right around the castle wall.

facts.text: Moats were not just clever, they were full of life. In 1292 King Edward I sent lots of young pike to live in the Tower of London's moat as a fish farm, and archaeologists later found a centuries-old wicker fish trap there with fish skeletons still inside.
facts.artAlt: A large pike swimming among green reeds in clear water
facts.caption: A pike, the fish King Edward put in the Tower's moat.

infographic.title: How wide was the moat?

rows.label: A school bus, end to end
A football field, side to side

infographic.caption: The Tower of London's moat width comes from Historic Royal Palaces. A football field is 160 feet from sideline to sideline, so the moat was about as wide as a whole field.

pages.title: Pictures That Say Your Name
pages.artAlt: A colorful medieval tapestry and a knight's shield hang on a stone castle wall

facts.text: When knights began wearing helmets that covered their faces, nobody could tell who was who. So each knight painted his own special mix of colors, shapes and animals on his shield and banners, a bit like writing your name in pictures.
Only one person was allowed to use each coat of arms. If you spotted a knight's design at a tournament, you knew exactly who was inside the armor, even if you could not see his face.
facts.artAlt: A medieval knight's shield painted with a bold heraldic design hanging on a stone castle wall
facts.caption: One shield, one design, one knight.

facts.text: Tapestries were woven from wool and silk threads by craftsmen with amazing skill, and they were the great art of their day. Covering a wall with them showed visitors that the owner was someone very grand indeed.
facts.artAlt: A large medieval woven tapestry covering a stone castle wall in warm light
facts.caption: A tapestry covering a whole stone wall.

infographic.title: Why knights painted their shields
